To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the coloration of greenfinches' tail feathers reflects the carotenoids they contain, and that the most colorful greenfinches deposit the most carotenoids into their feathers.
the carotenoid content in feathers of greenfinches is related to the colour of the feathers.

carotenoid content of feathers can be accurately inferred from the coloration of the feathers, that the coloration of feathers is a reliable indicator of the amount of carotenoid deposited into the feathers, and that the amount of carotonoid deposited into feathers is related to the amount of caroteneoid in the diet of the birds.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how birds obtain and allocate carotenoids to their plumage.
the relationship between carotinoids and plumage colour in birds.
the relationship between carotinoid-based colouration and the amount of carotenoid pigmentation present in the feathers of the greenfinch (Carduelis chloris).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
carotenoid-based colour signals in greenfinch tail feathers are honest indicators of the total amount of these pigments contained therein.
carotenoid-based colouration of plumage is a good indicator of total feather carotenoid concentration.
carotenoid-based colour signals can indeed be reliable indicators of the total carotenoid content of a bird's feathers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
carotenoid-based plumage signals are reliable, but only if the colour is assessed properly.

the coloration of carotenoid‐based feathers directly reflects their carotenoid content, and that the amount of carotenoid deposited in feathers is a function of the total amount of xanthophyll available to the bird.

the colour of carotenoid-containing feathers is an honest signal of the amount of carotenoid deposited into them, and that the deposition of carotenoid is not a limiting resource in the production of carotenoid‐based plumage signals.

carotenoid content is a better indicator of male quality than carotenoid colour.
